<reason>Both sides were strong and evenly matched through most rounds: A's "robust means a live veto over lawful code" and "the ask is inaudible after stripping" clashed effectively with B's spam-filter analogy and "the page can still ask." The decisive edge came late. B answered A's pressure questions squarely (A1/A2 on list-writing liability and the audible ask), then closed by crystallizing the one asymmetry A never resolved: why reversibility is a flaw in the protective default but was never demanded of the invasive one, plus the trap that A's own fallback (data rules) concedes regulation is needed and only relocates control. A's rebuttals were sharp—the first-party loophole and small-browser burden remained partially live—but A's "these defaults are not twins" distinction was asserted more than weighed, and B's closing labeled it exactly that way. A minor clipped closing sentence in B's Rebuttal 2 is the only execution cost. B made the debate marginally easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2 answer to "what carries the ask": the publisher can display a direct, visible request to allow tracking, so the complaint reduces to fear that users will say no—"a defense of revenue built on inattention"—which reframed A's entire prior-filter argument.</best_rebuttal>
